B1.title: A real news story in simpler English
B1.intro: This is real news, written for learners. The English is genuine but the pace is gentle. Pick any story from today.
comprehension: What is the main event or topic of the story you chose?
Where and when did it happen?
Name two facts the writer gives to support the main idea.
Why do you think this story is important to the people involved?
B1.vocab_task: Find 5 new words. Write each word, guess its meaning from the sentence, then check a dictionary.
B1.summary_task: Write 4-5 sentences retelling the story in your own words. Do not copy sentences from the article.

B1.title: 6 Minute English podcast
B1.intro: Two real BBC presenters discuss one topic for six minutes. Listen once for the general idea, then again with the transcript.
comprehension: What question do the presenters ask at the start?
What was the answer to their quiz question?
Explain two of the vocabulary words they taught in this episode.
Do you agree with the opinions the speakers shared? Why or why not?
B1.vocab_task: The episode teaches 5-6 words. Write them down with the example sentence the presenters used.
B1.summary_task: In 4-5 sentences, tell a friend what this episode was about and one thing you learned.

B1.title: The danger of a single story
B1.intro: A Nigerian writer explains how one story about a place or people can be misleading. Turn on English subtitles. This speaker is clear and slow.
comprehension: What does the speaker mean by 'a single story'?
Give one example she uses from her own life.
How can a single story create a stereotype?
What is one 'single story' people sometimes believe about your country?
B1.vocab_task: Find 5 words or phrases you did not know. Note the time in the video where you heard each one.
B1.summary_task: Write 5-6 sentences: what is the speaker's main message, and why does it matter?

B2.title: A full BBC news article
B2.intro: This is native-speed journalism — no simplification. Choose a longer article (not a short update) on a topic you care about.
comprehension: Summarise the article's main argument or event in one sentence.
What evidence or sources does the journalist use?
Identify one fact and one opinion in the article.
What information do you think was left out, and why might that matter?
B2.vocab_task: Collect 6 words or collocations that are new or used in an unfamiliar way. Write your own sentence for each.
B2.summary_task: Write a 6-8 sentence summary suitable for someone who has not read the article.

B2.title: Your body language may shape who you are
B2.intro: A social psychologist argues that how we stand can change how we feel. Watch at full speed if you can; use subtitles only when stuck.
comprehension: What is the speaker's central claim about 'power posing'?
How does she support the claim — what experiment does she describe?
What is the personal story she tells near the end?
Are you convinced by her argument? What would make it stronger?
B2.vocab_task: Note 6 academic or descriptive words. For each, write a synonym and an antonym.
B2.summary_task: Write an 8-sentence summary that explains both her claim and her evidence.

B2.title: A Guardian long read
B2.intro: Long-form journalism on one topic in depth. These essays use rich vocabulary and complex sentences — exactly the stretch you need.
comprehension: What is the writer's thesis (main point of view)?
How is the article structured — how does it move from start to finish?
Find two places where the writer uses a story or example to make a point.
What counter-arguments, if any, does the writer address?
B2.vocab_task: Choose 8 advanced words. Group them: which are formal, which are figurative (metaphor/idiom)?
B2.summary_task: Write a paragraph (8-10 sentences) summarising the argument and your reaction to it.

C1.title: An analytical article on world affairs
C1.intro: Dense, argument-driven writing with a distinctive voice and dry humour. Read an article to the end and follow the line of reasoning.
comprehension: State the article's argument in one precise sentence.
Trace the reasoning: what are the two or three steps that lead to the conclusion?
Where does the writer use irony, understatement, or wit? Quote it.
What assumption underlies the argument? Would you challenge it?
C1.vocab_task: Collect 8-10 items: advanced vocabulary, idioms, and any culturally specific references. Explain each.
C1.summary_task: Write a critical response (10-12 sentences): summarise the argument, then evaluate whether it holds up.

C1.title: How great leaders inspire action
C1.intro: A fast, rhetorical talk built on a single model ('start with why'). Follow the rhetoric at native speed and notice how he persuades.
comprehension: Explain the 'golden circle' model in your own words.
What examples does he use, and why does he choose them?
Identify two rhetorical techniques (repetition, contrast, rhetorical question, etc.) and where he uses them.
How persuasive is the talk? Distinguish the strength of the idea from the strength of the delivery.
C1.vocab_task: Note 8 phrases used for persuasion or emphasis. Mark which you could use in a presentation of your own.
C1.summary_task: Write a 10-12 sentence analysis of both what he argues and how he argues it.

C1.title: A chapter of classic literature
C1.intro: Read one chapter of a classic novel (try Orwell, Austen, or Dickens). Literary English stretches you further than any news article.
comprehension: What happens in the chapter, and from whose point of view is it told?
Describe the tone or mood. What creates it?
Find a sentence whose meaning depends on style (irony, metaphor, long syntax). Unpack it.
What does this chapter suggest about the writer's world or values?
C1.vocab_task: Collect 10 words: some archaic/literary, some still current. Note which you would actually use today.
C1.summary_task: Write a literary response (12-15 sentences): what happened, and what the writing does well.
